nuggets.summary: When a novice angel hears a plausible pitch, the instinctive reaction is to imagine everything that could go right — Gadre argues this is backwards. The useful diagnostic question is the opposite one: before writing the check, map out specifically where and why this venture is most likely to fail. Because almost any idea sounds plausible and exciting in the moment, optimism alone doesn't discriminate between good and bad bets; actively hunting for the failure points is what gives you a realistic read on whether the team can actually survive them.
nuggets.quote: in reality, like, what you need to think about is how could this thing go wrong, right? Because, you know, everything could happen, or everything is plausible... but, you know, what you really need to think about before you write your check is, okay, where is this thing going to fall down? Like, where are the failure points?

nuggets.summary: With 70 companies in his portfolio, Gadre can't meaningfully engage with all of them every week, so he manages attention using a rough bell-curve heuristic: at any given time only about ten of the portfolio companies actually need his help (an intro, a hire, bridge funding), and he concentrates on that subset while the rest cycle in as new needs arise. His rule for the companies not currently asking for anything is passive: he assumes they'll reach out if they need him, and if they don't call, he doesn't call them. This is a scalable way to triage founder support across a large portfolio without spreading yourself thin on companies that are currently fine.
nuggets.quote: there's sort of a bell curve of anything, right, and so, at any given point in time, out of those seven investments, maybe ten will need some help... those ten kind of cycle through, so... I essentially treat others, and I focus on the ones that need help right now, and then as those cycle out, somebody else cycles in, so I sort of focus on... the ones that don't need help, I assume they'll call me if they need help, and if they don't call me, then I'm not calling them

nuggets.summary: One of the most common red flags Gadre sees is a founder who is overly worried about dilution when more capital is on the table — turning down or hesitating on available money to preserve ownership percentage. His framing: because startups almost always take longer and cost more than founders expect, a large stake in a company that runs out of money is worth nothing, so it's rational to take money when it's offered even on imperfect terms rather than optimize for a bigger slice of an equity pie that may not survive. This matters even more in Seattle specifically, where funding can disappear entirely in a downturn (he cites 2008–2009 as effectively un-fundable locally) unlike the Valley, where capital tends to keep flowing even in a bad market.
nuggets.quote: a founder is too worried about dilution at the early stages, just a huge red flag, right? Because the reality is, everything that's going to take longer and costs more than you think it's going to... a large piece of a non-existent pie is not going to... be all that rewarding for you, you know, you'd much rather have a smaller piece of a bigger pie... especially in Seattle... the market downturn could really hammer this, you know, whereas in the Valley, you might still be able to get funded even in a nuclear winter, like a 2008 style... kind of scenario up here, like, forget it, like, nothing's getting funded in 2008, 2009

nuggets.summary: Gadre lays out a concrete, stage-based valuation rubric he's seen hold as the going market rate in Seattle over several years: a credible team with just an idea and no product is valued around $0–2M; a credible team with a built product but no go-to-market yet is $2–4M; a credible team showing early traction/proof points is $4–6M; and a credible team with a product already live in market is essentially uncapped ("the sky's the limit"). He uses this rubric directly with founders as an anchoring tool in valuation conversations, telling them plainly where the market says their stage sits before proposing a number.
nuggets.quote: sort of credible team with an idea, but no product out yet... the valuation is probably between zero and two million dollars... A credible team that has a product, but hasn't really gone to market... that value is sort of between two and four million dollars, and then a credible team that has the beginnings of traction... that's sort of four to six, and then if you have a credible team and they've got a product that's out in the market, it's like... the size of the limit

nuggets.summary: For a typical Seattle seed round, Gadre puts the standard dilution range for angels at 20–30%. He also flags a specific structural red flag beyond the headline number: angels who try to stack extra liquidation preferences on top of a clean deal. His advice to founders is to avoid investors pushing multiple layers of preference (e.g. a 3x liquidation preference), because it creates founder-motivation problems later and gives subsequent investors leverage to demand similarly aggressive terms — a clean 1x preference or a note converting at a reasonable cap is the healthier norm.
nuggets.quote: typically, you know, between 20 and 30 percent is kind of the... typical thing... I don't like this when angels try to layer on a bunch of... preferences... because it just causes a few problems down the road in terms of founder motivation, and then later investors... see that... and they want even more... you know, I would... stay away from anybody who's trying to... jam people

nuggets.summary: Gadre treats convertible notes as functionally equivalent to a priced round only up to about $1.5M in cumulative debt — past that threshold he advises founders to switch to pricing the round outright. His reasoning is concrete: carrying too much debt on the balance sheet can scare off certain downstream investors and complicate equipment-leasing type financing, and once a note has a valuation cap, it sets up a harder negotiation with the next round's investors over liquidation stacking. So the note-vs-priced-round choice isn't just about legal cost, it has real consequences for fundability a round or two later.
nuggets.quote: up to about a million and a half, you know, I think convertible notes are essentially fungible with price [rounds]... once you don't want to start wearing too much debt on the company because... certain types of investors won't... invest in the company [if it] has too much debt on the books... and then two... especially if there's a cap, it leads to tough discussions with your next funding partner

nuggets.summary: For marketplace startups specifically, Gadre says there is really only one variable that matters: liquidity, meaning whether the founder has a credible edge in seeding one side of the marketplace (supply or demand) so the other side follows. He states this is by far the hardest problem in any marketplace business, because sellers won't show up without buyers and buyers won't show up without sellers, so the two sides won't bootstrap each other on their own — someone needs an unfair advantage in cold-starting one side. He explicitly says this is his sole investment filter for marketplace pitches; without a clear liquidity-seeding edge, he passes regardless of the rest of the pitch.
nuggets.quote: the only thing that's important to the marketplace [is] the liquidity... the only times I'll invest in the marketplace is I feel like the founder has some edge in terms of building liquidity on one side or another to the marketplace... by far the hardest problem in any marketplace is finding a way to build liquidity on one side, because... sellers don't want to come unless there's buyers, and the buyers don't want to come unless there's sellers

nuggets.summary: Gadre frames the investor-founder relationship as functionally a multi-year marriage that depends on trust, and says the single fastest way to destroy that trust is over-promising and under-delivering — even a single detectable exaggeration during the pitch, not just an outright lie. Once an investor senses a founder has "folded" on credibility, the relationship is effectively over and no further progress is possible with that investor. The practical implication: sell the vision hard enough to convey why the opportunity is compelling, but never make a specific claim you can't back up, because the cost of getting caught is disproportionate to any short-term benefit of oversell.
nuggets.quote: investor and entrepreneur relationships are in a relationship, like a marriage... there has to be trust in that relationship... if you start over-promising and under-delivering, your credibility... immediately starts to go down... once an angel or any investor really gets the sense that this guy's kind of folded... you're done

nuggets.summary: When evaluating what makes a pitch compelling, Gadre draws a sharp line between ideas that are qualitatively / order-of-magnitude better than existing alternatives (or that create a category that doesn't exist yet) versus incremental improvements framed as percentage gains over a known competitor. He explicitly contrasts "we're 10% better than Google" (weak, hard to raise on) against something so categorically superior that customers feel they must have it. The actionable filter for founders: pitch the qualitative leap, not the incremental optimization, because incremental framing reads as a much harder sell to an investor even if the underlying business is fine.
nuggets.quote: I want to see something that is qualitatively, like, orders of magnitude better than [existing] solutions or maybe it doesn't even exist, right, there's nothing like this anywhere... that kind of thing is much more compelling than we're a slightly better version of this, you know, we're going to cut costs by 10%

nuggets.summary: Gadre uses his own reaction to first seeing Airbnb as a cautionary story against his usual filters: his gut instinct was to dismiss it outright because hotels already existed and solved the same basic need. What he initially failed to appreciate was that living in someone's actual apartment is a qualitatively different experience from a hotel room, not just a cheaper substitute for one — a distinction that wasn't obvious from the pitch alone and that he says he would have missed even if he'd had the chance to invest. It's a concrete admission that "this doesn't make sense because [obvious incumbent] already exists" is not a reliable disqualifier.
nuggets.quote: honestly, Airbnb... when I first saw it, I was like, really, I was like, no way... this thing, because it doesn't make any sense, because there's already hotels out there... but what I didn't appreciate is that there's a qualitatively different experience in living in somebody's apartment than there is living in [a] hotel[]

nuggets.summary: Asked for the single biggest thing founders should never say in a first pitch meeting, Gadre points to unsubstantiated, sales-flavored bravado — his example is a founder claiming they're "going to replace Google." The issue isn't ambition itself, it's making a specific claim that can't be backed up under questioning; once an investor catches that gap between claim and substance, the credibility damage is immediate and hard to recover from within that meeting.
nuggets.quote: it's probably something... anything that seems like just sales BS, right, you know, it's like, you know, we're going to... just [replace] Google, like, great... anything that just sounds like it just can't be substantiated, like, come on, like, you know, if... you damage the credibility like that, then that's... obviously not going to work too well

nuggets.summary: Gadre gives a specific, business-model-dependent set of numbers founders must be ready to defend in diligence. For transactional/enterprise businesses (anything selling at a price point), the core question is customer acquisition cost versus lifetime value of the customer — he calls this "the only thing that matters in the long run." For growth/engagement/advertising-based businesses where per-user revenue is thin, the founder instead needs a credible answer for how growth happens virally or through free distribution partnerships, since they can't afford to pay for acquisition at all. Not knowing your own numbers on this axis — or knowing them less well than the investor questioning you — is presented as an immediate disqualifier.
nuggets.quote: for enterprise companies... or any... company that's based on transactions... the key dynamic that you have to understand is what is the cost of customer acquisition... and how does that compare to the lifetime value of the customer, because that's it, that's the only thing that matters in the long run... for companies that are based on... growth and engagement and advertising... you can't afford to pay anything to [acquire] these users, so you need to find a way to make that... hockey stick... happen... virally or through distribution partners

nuggets.summary: Gadre says he makes investment go/no-go decisions quickly rather than dragging out due diligence, on the philosophy that a fast rejection respects both parties' time more than a prolonged maybe. The specific line he cites — "a quick no is the second best answer" — reframes speed of decision-making itself as a form of investor courtesy and professionalism, not just personal efficiency, worth naming explicitly to founders who might otherwise read a fast pass as dismissive.
nuggets.quote: I don't think it serves anybody to drag things out... it just [wastes] the entrepreneur's time, it [wastes] my time... as they say, a quick no is the second best answer

nuggets.summary: Gadre offers a structural explanation for why he finds Seattle's investing culture markedly more cooperative and collegial than the Valley's, one that runs counter to the assumption that more money in an ecosystem makes it friendlier. In the Valley, there's so much capital chasing a relatively small number of good deals that competition among investors turns cutthroat. In Seattle, the ratio is inverted — more companies than available funding — which paradoxically produces more collaboration among investors rather than more competition. He explicitly predicts this would flip if Valley-scale money started flooding into Seattle.
nuggets.quote: in the valley, there's so much money chasing... relatively fewer deals, whereas up here, it's the opposite problem, where you have more companies than there is funding, and so here... the investment culture is much more cooperative, much more collaborative... that would change... if we got wildly successful, and all of a sudden, valley money started flooding in

nuggets.summary: Gadre has a specific historical theory for why so few early Amazon employees became active local angel investors or startup founders in Seattle, despite the company producing significant wealth. His account: during the dot-com bust, the early Amazon cohort who might have left to found companies couldn't get funded because there was no capital available at the time, and by the time the market recovered it was too late for many of them — they'd settled into "pioneer, then settler" roles inside a now-large company rather than founders. He notes this pattern is now reversing: he's increasingly seeing people do only two-to-four-year stints at Amazon before leaving to start something, unlike the earlier "old guard" who mostly stayed.
nuggets.quote: during the dot-com bust, when... a lot of the early Amazon employees would have been out founding companies, they couldn't get funded because there was no money. And then by the time... they finally recovered, it was kind of too late for them... but now, actually, I'm starting to see... a lot of people who will do... two or three, four years at Amazon and then peel off and do a start-up

nuggets.summary: Gadre describes a deliberate geographic arbitrage strategy behind joining Founders Co-op: source seed deals in Seattle at valuations well below Bay Area norms, then use strong Bay Area connections to help the winners raise follow-on rounds at Valley-style valuations. The mechanism only works if the fund has real downstream connectivity to Valley capital — otherwise a cheap Seattle entry price is just a cheap entry price, not an arbitrage. This is a specific, replicable thesis for why investing in an underpriced regional market can outperform investing directly in an expensive one, provided you can bridge the two markets at the follow-on stage.
nuggets.quote: there's actually a very interesting arbitrage between Seattle and the Bay Area, in that... if you can find good [seed] deals in Seattle and invest in them at... not Valley prices... if you're significantly connected down to the Bay Area... hopefully the ones of those that are successful, you can take them and get... significant up rounds... more Valley-style valuations
